newsitem.title: USA: U.S. housing affordability slips in Q2--NAR.
newsitem.headline: U.S. housing affordability slips in Q2--NAR.

text.p: U.S. homes were slightly less affordable in the second quarter of 1997 than in the first quarter, but housing affordability conditions remain favourable, the National Association of Realtors said Thursday.

The real estate industry group's housing affordability index slipped to 125.5 in the second quarter from 130.8 in the first quarter, NAR said. It was also down slightly from 125.7 a year earlier, in the second quarter of 1996.

When the NAR index measures 100, a family earning the median income has exactly the amount needed to buy a single-family home at the median price, using conventional financing and a 20 percent down payment.
Although the index fell in the second quarter, NAR noted that affordability is still on the upswing due to low mortgage rates and an overall healthy economy.
"We expect affordability conditions to remain favourable in the months ahead for both move-up and first-time purchasers," NAR President Russell Booth said in a statement.

In the second quarter, the median home price was $123,700, median family income was $43,291 and mortgage rates averaged 7.89 percent. In the first quarter, the median home price was $119,400, the median family income was $42,838 and mortgage rates averaged 7.72 percent.

The NAR's Housing Affordability Index measures the ability of a family earning the median income to buy a home at the median price. Half the nation's potential home buyers earn more than $43,291 a year and half earn less.
Qualifying income for conventional financing was $34,491 in the second quarter, up from $32,752 in the prior quarter.

The NAR said the first-time buyer index, which shows the ability of renters to qualify for a mortgage, fell in the second quarter to 79.9 from 83.2 in the first quarter. It was unchanged from the second quarter of 1996.
The median price of a starter home rose in the second quarter to $105,100 from $101,500 in the prior quarter.
Booth noted that a tax provision is expected to be approved by Congress that will permit penalty-free withdrawals for the purchase of a starter home from tax-deferred savings accounts.
He said the provision will narrow the affordability gap for first-time buyers as it "addresses a major obstacle to home ownership, which is the inability to accumulate a sufficient down payment."
